items: Spring Caching Mechanics: Both @MockBean and @SpyBean force the Spring TestContext framework to modify or create a new ApplicationContext. Because Spring caches application contexts across tests to optimize execution speed, introducing a mock bean with unique configurations can invalidate the context cache, triggering expensive context reloads.

Partial Mocking Gotchas with @SpyBean: When calling real methods on a @SpyBean using Mockito.when(spy.method()).thenReturn(val), Mockito actually evaluates the real method first before applying the stub. If the real method has side effects, throws an uninitialized NullPointerException, or queries an unmocked database, it will fail. Always use doReturn(val).when(spy).method() syntax with spies to avoid premature execution.

Name vs. Type Resolution: If multiple beans of the same type exist in the ApplicationContext, both annotations will throw an AmbiguousBeanDefinitionException unless you explicitly narrow down the target using the name or qualifier attributes provided by the annotation.

parsed_answer.content: A frequent production trap in large test suites is the over-reliance on @MockBean, which leads to 'test pollution' and bloated context caches. Every unique combination of @MockBean declarations forces Spring to spin up a brand new ApplicationContext. If you have 50 test classes each declaring a slightly different set of mock beans, Spring might boot up 50 separate contexts, causing your test suite execution time to skyrocket. Prefer unit tests with pure Mockito (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) for isolated logic, and reserve @MockBean and @SpyBean strictly for true integration boundaries.
